nodes.label: Regtest halves every 150 blocks
nodes.body: On mainnet the block reward halves every 210,000 blocks, about four years; on regtest the interval is only 150, so that a developer can see several halvings within a few minutes (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The test chain showed the reward through getblockstats: 50 coins at heights 1 and 149, 25 at 150 and 299, 12.5 at 300 and 449, and 6.25 at 450 and 500, the same values as the code's subsidy rule with the interval 150 (Bitcoin Core, 2026). The book does not mention the interval, but it leads to the balance in the next listing.

nodes.label: Regtest balance after 500 blocks
nodes.body: The book mines 500 blocks on regtest and finds a balance of 12,462.5 coins, because the rewards must be 100 blocks deep to be spent (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The book's number is correct, and it is correct only because of the interval of 150.

nodes.label: No default wallet
nodes.body: The book's regtest session begins with the command createwallet with an empty name, to make a default wallet, but a Bitcoin Core 31.1 node refuses it: the command printed the error 'Wallet name cannot be empty' and exited with code 8 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Release 31.0 mentions the empty wallet name in a different place, the Restore Wallet dialog of the graphical interface, which shows an error if the name is empty (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).

nodes.label: Development pipeline
nodes.body: This subject asks how the test chains are used together: from regtest to signet or testnet and then to mainnet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). This subject covers Pipeline order.

nodes.label: Pipeline order
nodes.body: The book recommends a development pipeline: test the code on regtest, then on signet or testnet, and finally put it into production on mainnet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The source shows how the stages differ in how public they are: regtest has one dummy seed and no peers, signet has 2 DNS seeds and a block rule that needs a signature, testnet3 has 5 seeds and the minimum-difficulty rule, and mainnet has 8 seeds and no such rule (Bitcoin Core, 2026). A developer meets more and more of the real world at each step, other software, other people's transactions and network delays.
nodes.definition: The three stages differ in what the code gives them: regtest has one dummy seed and no public peers, signet 2 seeds and a signed block rule, testnet3 5 seeds and the minimum-difficulty rule, mainnet 8 seeds, the order the book recommends.

has component (hasComponent, a relationship of category Compositional) in the chapter's research: A block is a container: a small header, then a counter, then the transactions (Block is header plus transactions); the header is exactly 80 bytes (The header is 80 bytes).

has component (hasComponent, a relationship of category Compositional) in the chapter's research: The 80 bytes of the header are 4 for the version, 32 for the previous block hash, 32 for the merkle root (The header is 80 bytes); the root is the single 32-byte summary of the transactions in the header (Root is always32 bytes).

has component (hasComponent, a relationship of category Compositional) in the chapter's research: A merkleblock message holds the header and a merkle path, 248 bytes of which 80 are the header (Merkleblock for light clients); the fixed size of the header makes light clients possible (The header is 80 bytes).

has consequence (hasConsequence, a relationship of category Causal) in the chapter's research: Because the previous-block field is part of the header and so of the hash, changing a block changes its own hash and breaks the link in the next block (Tampering breaks descendants; Block hash is double sha256).

has consequence (hasConsequence, a relationship of category Causal) in the chapter's research: The zeros of a block hash are the visible result of the rule that the hash, read as a number, must not exceed the target (Hash leading zeros); the header stores the target in 4 bytes (Target compact encoding).

findings: Background

The chapter describes the blockchain as an ordered, back-linked list of blocks in which every block commits to its parent through the previous-block hash of its header (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023). The description is confirmed by a real pair of blocks: block 277,315 has the parent hash of block 277,314, version 2, time 1388185038, nonce 4215469401 and merkle root 5e049f40..., the values of the book's listing, with 40 transactions in 43,560 bytes (Mempool Space, 2026). The block hash is the one-line double SHA-256 of the 80-byte header in the code (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Background

The header is 80 bytes and a block may be 4,000,000 bytes, so a block can be 50,000 times the size of its header, as the book says (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); the constant MAX_BLOCK_SERIALIZED_SIZE is 4,000,000 and the header class has the six fields in the order of the book's table (Bitcoin Core, 2026). Today the 971,538 headers of the main chain take about 78 megabytes at 80 bytes each, against a whole chain of 775,272 megabytes (Blockchain Charts, 2026).
Comparative analysis

Erratum of arithmetic: the book says that the largest possible merkle proof is almost 10,000 times smaller than the largest block. The proof needs the 80-byte header and 448 bytes of path, 528 bytes, so a block of 4,000,000 bytes is 7,576 times larger; with a typical 250-byte transaction the ratio is 5,141, and 10,000 would need a proof of 400 bytes. The statement that a path has 10 to 14 hashes (320 to 448 bytes) is right (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The design flaw in the merkle tree is real and has a history: the comment in merkle.cpp warns of CVE-2012-2459, Optech states that the vulnerability was reported in 2012 and fixed quietly, that a variation was reintroduced in 0.13.0 in 2016 and fixed in 0.14.0, and that another was found in 2023; on the test chain a block with a repeated last transaction had the same header and hash and was rejected as bad-txns-duplicate, after which the genuine block was accepted (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The book does not mention the second weakness of the tree: an inner node is the hash of 64 bytes, and a transaction of exactly 64 bytes without witness data can be mistaken for one, which Optech lists as CVE-2017-12842. BIP 54, the consensus cleanup, would make such transactions invalid, which fixes the weakness for light clients without a workaround (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The weight limit is the real block limit: MAX_BLOCK_WEIGHT is 4,000,000 weight units and block 840,000 held 3,993,281 weight units in 2,325,617 bytes. Block templates of Bitcoin Core stop at 3,992,000 because 8,000 units are reserved (-blockreservedweight), and release 29.0 fixed a bug that had reserved the 4,000 units twice. The book says that transactions can total about 4,000,000 bytes (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Changed output: the getblock listing of the book has no target and no coinbase_tx. Bitcoin Core 29.0 added the field target to getblock and getblockheader and 31.0 added the coinbase_tx object, and the genesis block of the test chain showed both (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The version field is no longer a version number: BIP 9 requires the top three bits 001 for blocks that signal, giving the range from 0x20000000, and the draft BIP 320 reserves sixteen bits (mask 0x1fffe000) for general use, with BIP 323 proposed as its replacement. Block 840,000 carries 0x2a5fe000 and the blocks of the test chain 0x20000000, while the book says only that the field's use has evolved (Wuille et al., 2015); (BtcDrak, 2018); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

Timewarp and testnet storms have shaped recent releases. BIP 94 for testnet4 starts the retarget from the first block of the previous period and bounds the time of the first block of a period to 600 seconds before its parent; Bitcoin Core 29.0 made block templates respect the timewarp rule on all networks and turned the rule off on regtest, and the consensus cleanup of BIP 54 would apply a timewarp fix to mainnet, which Optech's time warp topic explains (Jahr, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2025); (Poinsot and Corallo, 2025); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Comparative analysis

The genesis block holds a first reward that can never be spent, a quirk that the Bitcoin Wiki says may or may not have been intended, and a node on the test chain confirmed that getrawtransaction refuses the genesis coinbase, gettxout returns nothing and the UTXO set at height 0 is empty. Testnet4 has its own genesis coinbase (180 bytes, id 7aa0a7ae...) with the message 03/May/2024; the book does not mention either point (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Jahr, 2024); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Comparative analysis

The timestamp is described by the book only as an approximate time. The rules are that it must be greater than the median of the previous 11 blocks (BIP 113) and not more than 2 hours ahead of the node's clock, and a 4-byte counter overflows on 2106-02-07; block 277,315 is 1,651 seconds later than its median time past (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Kerin and Friedenbach, 2015); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026); (Wikipedia contributors, 2026).
Comparative analysis

Heights have moved: the book reports height 800,000 in mid 2023, and on 2026-10-15 the main chain was at height 971,537; block 840,000, mined on 2024-04-20 at 00:09:27 UTC, is the first with the reward of 3.125 coins. The book's number of 12,462.5 coins after 500 blocks on regtest is right, because the regtest reward halves every 150 blocks and not every 210,000 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Conclusion

The ideas under the chapter are older than Bitcoin: Haber and Stornetta described hash-linked time-stamping in 1991, Ralph Merkle's hash tree dates from 1979 and described tree authentication in 1980, and Nakamoto's paper cites the first and uses the second for compressing old blocks (Haber and Stornetta, 1991); (Wikipedia contributors, 2026); (Merkle, 1980); (Nakamoto, 2008).
Conclusion

The probability that an attacker with 10 percent of the hash rate catches up from 6 blocks behind is 0.0002428, from 1 block behind 0.2045873, and with 30 percent at 6 blocks 0.1321, computed again with the formula of the paper; this is the quantitative reason behind the book's point that deeper blocks are more stable (Nakamoto, 2008); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Conclusion

Taken together, the chapter's account of the block, the chain and the merkle tree stands, and every structural claim could be recomputed. What is wrong or out of date lies at the edges: one arithmetic ratio, one sentence on testnet difficulty, the sizes and heights of 2023, the list of address prefixes, the testnet3 advice, the empty wallet name, and five changes of default or output since the book: XOR block files, testnet4, new getblock fields, signet magic by challenge and the reserved block weight (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Erratum for a reader who types the book's regtest session: the first command, createwallet with an empty name, is refused by Bitcoin Core 31.1 with the error 'Wallet name cannot be empty' (exit code 8), a fresh node has no wallet, and getnewaddress fails with 'No wallet is loaded'; the wallet needs a name (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed default: since release 28.0 the block files blk*.dat are scrambled with a random XOR key kept in blocks/xor.dat, and older releases and external software cannot read such a directory. In the run the first bytes of blk00000.dat were unreadable until the key d462ed9f917fe79d was applied, after which the file began with the magic fabfb5da and the size 285 of the genesis block. The book describes the blocks as plain data in the files (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).
Contemporary developments

The book's block table begins with a 4-byte block size, which is not part of a block as it travels or as consensus sees it but a field that Bitcoin Core writes in front of each block in its block files, after the magic bytes; on the test chain the genesis block took 293 bytes on disk, 285 plus 8 (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed state: the book names testnet3 as the current testnet, but Bitcoin Core 28.0 added testnet4 as specified in BIP 94 (assigned 2024-05-27 to Fabian Jahr, now Deployed), and Bitcoin Core 31.1 still starts testnet3 with -testnet while its help text says that the support is deprecated and will be removed; Optech calls testnet4 a recently started replacement (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Jahr, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2024); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2026); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Erratum of size: the book calls testnet3 a chain in excess of 30 GB, but Bitcoin Core 31.1 assumes 245 GB for it in chainparams.cpp, and on 2026-10-15 testnet3 stood at height 5,189,394, 6.3 times the number of blocks that one block in ten minutes since 2011-02-02 would have given and more than 5 times the 971,537 blocks of mainnet (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Mempool Space, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Erratum of detail: the book says that the minimum difficulty of testnet is half that of Bitcoin, but chainparams.cpp gives mainnet and testnet3 the same proof-of-work limit 00000000ffff..., so the minimum difficulty is 1 on both. The sentence agrees with the Bitcoin Wiki and not with the code. The second rule, that a block more than 20 minutes after its parent may use the minimum difficulty, is right (pow.cpp uses 2 x 10 minutes) and holds for testnet3, testnet4 and regtest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Bitcoin Wiki, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Incomplete list: the book's tip says that test networks use addresses beginning with m, n or tb1, but the test chains also use the prefix 2 for script-hash addresses (base58 version 196) and regtest uses bcrt1 (bech32 prefix bcrt), as its own listing shows; the nodes of the run produced m, 2, tb1q and tb1p on testnet4 and signet, and bcrt1q and bcrt1p on regtest (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

Changed value: the book's listing of the default signet shows 143,619 blocks and a size of 769,525,915 bytes and says that the default signet has about 150,000 blocks and is about a gigabyte; on 2026-10-15 its tip was at height 326,440, 2.27 times as many, and Bitcoin Core assumes 24 GB of disk space for it (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Mempool Space, 2026); (Bitcoin Core, 2026).
Contemporary developments

The default signet is operated by two contributors, as the book says, and the reason is visible in its challenge: a 71-byte script that is a 1-of-2 multisig of two 33-byte keys, so that either operator can sign a block. BIP 325 was assigned on 2019-03-20 to Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns, and Bitcoin Core 0.21.0 added the support with one public signet maintained (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023); (Alm and Towns, 2019); (Bitcoin Core developers, 2021); (Bitcoin Optech, 2026).
Contemporary developments

The message-start bytes of a signet are not constants but the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of the challenge script with its length byte in front, so every custom signet has its own network magic: 0a03cf40 for the default signet, 54d26fbd for the challenge 51 and 7ec653a5 for the example of BIP 325, which lists the same value. The book does not mention this (Bitcoin Core, 2026); (Alm and Towns, 2019); (Antonopoulos and Harding, 2023).

stories.title: The reward that was mined twice
stories.who: Pieter Wuille, who wrote BIP 30, Gavin Andresen, who wrote BIP 34, and the miners of blocks 91722, 91812, 91842 and 91880, whose names the chain does not record
stories.where: the Bitcoin chain (blocks 91722, 91812, 91842 and 91880), the Bitcoin Core source file validation.cpp and the bitcoin/bips repository
stories.story: On 14 November 2010 block 91812, mined at 17:59 UTC, paid its 50 coins in a coinbase transaction with the identifier d5d27987, and block 91842, mined three hours later, carried a coinbase with the same identifier. Blocks 91722 (14 November) and 91880 (15 November), mined about sixteen hours apart, repeated the identifier e3bf3d07 in the same way, because a coinbase has no input that could make it differ, so the same script and the same reward gave the same bytes, and a transaction is named by the hash of its bytes. Bitcoin Core marks the 50 coins of the earlier blocks 91722 and 91812 as unspendable, and its function IsBIP30Repeat lets the later blocks 91842 and 91880 through by their heights and hashes. In 2012 Pieter Wuille wrote BIP 30, which forbids a block to contain a transaction whose identifier matches an earlier transaction that is not fully spent, and Gavin Andresen wrote BIP 34, which puts the height of the block first in every coinbase script. Block 227,835 was the last version 1 block, the last that did not have to carry that height. In this chapter the height is read back from the coinbase scripts of eight blocks, and blocks 91842 and 91880 remain the only two that the rule against repeated identifiers lets through by exception.
stories.lesson: Put the height in the coinbase and no two coinbases can be equal

stories.title: One small hash that vouches for a whole list
stories.who: Ralph Merkle, the cryptographer who patented the hash tree, and Stanford University, the assignee of the patent
stories.where: Stanford University in California; United States patent 4309569, published on 5 January 1982
stories.story: Go back to Stanford University in California. Ralph Merkle's hash tree dates from 1979, and the United States patent 4309569, Method of providing digital signatures, was published on 5 January 1982 with the Board of Trustees of Stanford University as assignee. The patent explains both the tree and how it handles many one-time signatures, and in 1980 Merkle wrote about tree authentication in his paper Protocols for Public Key Cryptosystems. Decades later Satoshi Nakamoto's paper hashes the transactions of a block in a Merkle tree and keeps only the root in the block header, so that one small value vouches for a whole list. We followed it in this chapter: the 40 transaction ids of block 277,315 were hashed in pairs up six levels and gave the root 5e049f40..., the value in its header, and a path of 4 hashes proved one transaction among 16.
stories.lesson: A small summary can vouch for a large list

stories.title: When testnet was flooded with blocks
stories.who: Jameson Lopp, who wrote the blog post, and Fabian Jahr, who wrote BIP 94 for testnet4
stories.where: the blog of Jameson Lopp, the bitcoin/bips repository, and Bitcoin Core 28.0
stories.story: On 4 May 2024 Jameson Lopp published Griefing Bitcoin's Testnet, which describes how the testnet3 rule of minimum difficulty after 20 minutes lets miners create hundreds of blocks in a single day. The fix was testnet4: it had its genesis block on 3 May 2024 and BIP 94 was assigned to Fabian Jahr on 27 May 2024; it starts the retarget from the first block of the previous period and bounds the time of the first block of a period. Bitcoin Core 28.0 added the network with the option -testnet4. BIP 94 notes that three years' worth of blocks had been mined on testnet3 in a few weeks, and on 15 October 2026 testnet3 stood at height 5,189,394, against 156,618 on testnet4. Bitcoin Core 31.1 still starts testnet3 but says in its help that the support will be removed.
stories.lesson: A test network without incentives needs rules against vandals

stories.title: A test network where signatures replace mining
stories.who: Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns, the authors of BIP 325
stories.where: the bitcoin/bips repository, and Bitcoin Core 0.21.0
stories.story: BIP 325, Signet, was assigned on 20 March 2019 to Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns: a test network in which a block is valid only if it carries a solution to a challenge script, so that its creators decide who may make blocks. Bitcoin Core 0.21.0 added the support, with one public signet maintained and personal signets possible with -signetchallenge. The challenge of the default signet is a 1-of-2 multisig of two keys, and its four message-start bytes, 0a03cf40, are the start of the double SHA-256 of that script with its length byte in front. Its genesis block has the time 2020-09-01 00:00:00 UTC, and on 15 October 2026 its tip was at height 326,440, 2.27 times the 143,619 blocks of the book's listing. To see the other extreme, a signet that anyone could sign, with the challenge 51, ran on the test node of this chapter.
stories.lesson: Replace mining by a signature and a test network stays calm

lecture.title: Chapter 11: The Blockchain
lecture.say: This deck explains how a Bitcoin block is built, how blocks are linked and named, how a merkle tree lets one hash stand for many transactions, and how the test chains differ from the main chain. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library or read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core 31.1. Remember that a recorded run is one observation, not a general law. The seventeen code examples are listed in the same order in the Run slide code menu of the course page, where each one can be run and edited. The chapter follows the chapter on the blockchain in Mastering Bitcoin, third edition.
lecture.takeaway: How a block is built, how blocks are linked, how a merkle tree vouches for them, and which chain to test on

lecture.title: Today's route
lecture.say: The route opens with the questions and the concept map and then has three parts that follow the order of the chapter: the block and the chain, merkle trees, and test blockchains. The numbers on the right say what to expect: 43 slides, four true stories and seventeen code examples, each with a picture of its result. Every slide is numbered at the bottom right, so a topic is easy to find again. The examples appear in the same order in the Run slide code menu of the course page, so every listing here can be run and changed there. Use this slide to find where a topic lives.
lecture.takeaway: Three parts, seventeen examples, four true stories

lecture.title: The questions this chapter answers
lecture.say: Seven questions frame the chapter, and each is answered on a named slide: the six header fields on slide 9, how a block is named and placed on slides 16 and 17, why one old change breaks later blocks on slide 18, how one root stands for many transactions on slide 22, how short a membership proof is on slide 24, how testnet, signet and regtest differ on slides 30 to 40, and why testnet4 replaced testnet3 on slides 32 and 33. The summary on slide 41 returns to them. A reader who can answer all seven in their own words has understood the chapter, so try each question before opening its slide.
lecture.takeaway: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

lecture.title: One chapter, three parts
lecture.say: The concept map shows how the chapter is divided. The block and the chain carry 17 key concepts and 8 examples, merkle trees carry 7 key concepts and 4 examples, and test blockchains carry 17 key concepts and 5 examples, 41 key concepts in all. Each part opens with a divider, continues with concept cards, and proves its ideas with code and a true story. The concept cards are short revision stops: each gives a meaning and points to the example that shows the idea. Use the map to see which part to revisit when an idea feels unclear, and compare it with the taxonomy of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Three parts; every slide today lives on this map

lecture.title: The block and the chain
lecture.say: A block is a header of 80 bytes followed by a list of transactions. This part takes the header apart, shows how a block is named and placed in the chain, and explains why changing one old block breaks every later block. The three columns preview the part: the anatomy of a block with examples 1 to 3, names and positions with examples 4 to 6, and links and forks with examples 7 and 8. Remember that each block names its parent by hash; that single habit turns separate blocks into a chain. Chapter 10 of the course describes the network that passes the blocks around.
lecture.takeaway: Each block is tied to the one before it by that block's hash

lecture.title: The block and the chain: concepts (1 of 5)
lecture.say: These four cards define the vocabulary of a single block. A block is an 80-byte header, a count of transactions and then the transactions; the header holds six fixed fields that summarise what follows; a block has two names, the hash of its header and its height, which is its position counted from the genesis block; and the genesis block, mined on 3 January 2009, has no parent. Retell each card in your own words before moving on. Example 1 shows the structure, example 2 the header, examples 5 and 6 the two names and example 4 the genesis block. Compare with the chapter on the blockchain in Mastering Bitcoin.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: A block is header, count, transactions
lecture.say: The genesis block is the smallest block that matters: an 80-byte header, one count byte saying that there is one transaction, and a transaction of 204 bytes, 285 bytes in all. The code rebuilds the transaction from constants in Bitcoin Core's source, adds the three parts and compares the sum with the size that Bitcoin Core reports for its own genesis block on a private chain, a test chain run on one computer only for the examples and called regtest; the code slides read its recorded results as the record R. Two equal numbers from two independent sources are the proof. This is example 1 in the Run slide code menu of the course page. It connects to slide 9, which takes the 80-byte header apart field by field.
lecture.takeaway: Header, count byte and transaction make the whole block

lecture.title: The block and the chain: concepts (2 of 5)
lecture.say: These cards connect blocks into a chain. Each header holds the hash of its parent, so the blocks form one chain that every node keeps; a parent block is the block that a header names as the one before it; and the genesis block is the only block with no parent, its hash being fixed in the software. Because every link is a hash, a change to an old block changes its hash and breaks the link of the next block. Example 7 counts the links, example 8 shows two blocks that name the same parent, and example 4 shows the block without a parent. Compare with the fork on slide 19.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: Six fields in 80 bytes
lecture.say: A block header always has the same six fields in the same order: version, previous block hash, merkle root, time, bits and nonce. Their widths are 4, 32, 32, 4, 4 and 4 bytes, and 4 plus 32 plus 32 plus three times 4 make 80. The code cuts the header of block 480 on the private chain, the regtest chain of slide 7, at the positions 0, 4, 36, 68, 72, 76 and 80, so each width is the gap between two neighbouring cut points; it then reads the compact target, bits, from the same bytes and gets 207fffff. A fixed size makes headers cheap to store and check. This is example 2; the fields return in the merkle slides.
lecture.takeaway: Every header has the same six fields in the same order and widths

lecture.title: The block and the chain: concepts (3 of 5)
lecture.say: These cards prepare the fork example. Child blocks name an earlier block as their parent, and one parent may have several children; blocks are bundles of transactions with a header, added to the chain about every ten minutes; and the block header hash is the double SHA-256 of the 80 header bytes, which is the name of the block and is never printed inside it. Only one child continues the active chain. Example 8 shows two children of one parent and example 5 computes a block's name. Retell the difference between a block and its name in your own words.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: Time, target and difficulty
lecture.say: The header carries three numbers about time and work. The time field counts seconds since 1 January 1970; the median time past is the middle value of the last eleven timestamps, so one wrong clock cannot move it. Bits packs the target into four bytes, an exponent and three digit bytes: 1d00ffff means 0xffff times 256 to the power 26, a number of 224 bits, and it is the easiest target. Difficulty is that easiest target divided by the current one. In the result the genesis time is 2009-01-03 18:15:05, the median time past is 1792052132, and the difficulty of bits 1903a30c is 1,180,923,195. A smaller target means more work. This is example 3.
lecture.takeaway: Bits is a compressed target; a smaller target means more difficulty

lecture.title: The block and the chain: concepts (4 of 5)
lecture.say: Block height is the number of blocks between a block and the genesis block, so the genesis block sits at height 0. Bitcoin Core is the reference software that checks every rule and stores the chain; in this chapter its recorded results are the reference against which the chapter's own code is compared. Satoshi Nakamoto is the pseudonymous creator of Bitcoin, who wrote the 2008 paper and mined the first block. Nobody knows who is behind the name. Connect height with slide 17, where the height of a block is decoded from the first script of the block.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: The first block quotes a newspaper
lecture.say: The first block quotes a newspaper headline: The Times of 3 January 2009, Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks, a message of 69 characters stored in the source code. The block's name, 000000000019d668 and so on, starts with ten zero digits, which shows that very many nonces were tried before this header was found; that effort is the proof of work, and it is why the block is costly to forge. The time field is 1231006505. This is example 4; the next slide tells the story of two blocks that repeated a coinbase.
lecture.takeaway: The ten zeros at the start of the name are the proof of work

lecture.title: Two blocks with one coinbase
lecture.say: On 14 November 2010 block 91812 paid its 50 coins in a coinbase transaction named d5d27987, and block 91842, mined about three hours later, carried a coinbase with the same bytes and therefore the same name; blocks 91722 (14 November) and 91880 (15 November) did the same with the name e3bf3d07. A coinbase has no input that could make it differ, so equal scripts and equal rewards gave equal bytes, and a transaction is named by the hash of its bytes. The later copy overwrote the earlier coins, which Bitcoin Core marks by listing the earlier two blocks as unspendable and the later two as allowed repeats. Pieter Wuille's BIP 30 of 2012 forbids a block to repeat the name of an unspent transaction, and Gavin Andresen's BIP 34 puts the height first in every coinbase script. See slide 17.
lecture.takeaway: The reward that was mined twice

lecture.title: The block and the chain: concepts (5 of 5)
lecture.say: These cards close the first part. Linking blocks means that each block commits to its parent's hash, so rewriting history means redoing the work of all later blocks. BIP 34 is the proposal that puts the block height at the start of every coinbase script, so anyone can read a block's position from its first transaction. The Bitcoin network is the peer-to-peer system of nodes that relay blocks and transactions; chapter 10 of the course describes it. Example 7 shows the cost of changing a block and example 6 reads BIP 34 heights. Retell how the three ideas depend on each other.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: Hash twice to get the name
lecture.say: A block is named by hashing its 80-byte header twice with SHA-256. The code hashes once and gets a value that starts with 6dd6c5716cc8, which does not match the block's name; the second hash, taken over the first, starts with the zeros of the name and equals the hash in Bitcoin Core's source. The slice [::-1] reverses the bytes, because a block name is displayed in the opposite byte order to the raw hash. The name is stored nowhere inside the block: every node recomputes it, so a name cannot be faked without doing the work. This is example 5. Compare with the ten zeros on slide 13 and with the parent link on slide 18.
lecture.takeaway: The name is computed again by every node; it is never stored in the block

lecture.title: Height in the coinbase script
lecture.say: Since BIP 34 the first bytes of the coinbase script carry the block's height, so no two coinbases can have the same bytes and the same name, the repeat told on slide 14. The code reads back the heights 1, 16, 17, 127, 128, 255, 256 and 500, chosen at the borders of the encoding: 1 to 16 are a single opcode, and any other height is a length byte followed by the number in little-endian order, which needs a second byte from 128 up. Maturity is the second part: a coinbase reward may be spent only after 100 confirmations, and Bitcoin Core refused it after 99 and accepted it after 100. The wait guards against a block later replaced by another branch, as on slide 19. This is example 6.
lecture.takeaway: A newly mined reward cannot be spent until 100 blocks are on top of it

lecture.title: Changing one block breaks the chain
lecture.say: Each header holds the hash of its parent. In ten consecutive headers of the private chain nine links hold. When one bit in header 3 is flipped, the hash of header 3 changes, the link at header 4 breaks, and seven headers have to be mined again to make the chain valid. That cost is what protects old blocks: the older a block is, the more work an attacker must redo. This is example 7, the most important example of the part. It connects to slide 19, where two branches compete and the longer one becomes the active chain.
lecture.takeaway: Alter block 3 and you must mine seven headers again

lecture.title: A fork, and the odds of catching up
lecture.say: Two blocks mined on the same parent at height 511 form a fork, and the branch with more work wins. The white paper uses the same race to price an attack: the attacker finds a block with probability q, here 0.1, the honest miners with p, here 0.9. With z blocks gained by the honest chain and λ = zq/p, the chance of ever catching up is P = 1 − Σ (λ^k · e^−λ / k!) · (1 − (q/p)^(z−k)), summed over k = 0 to z. The first factor is the Poisson chance that the attacker found k blocks meanwhile; the second is the chance of closing the remaining deficit. P is 1.0, 0.2045873, 0.0509779 and 0.0002428 for z of 0, 1, 2 and 6. This is example 8.
lecture.takeaway: A fork ends when one branch grows longer; an attacker's odds fall fast

lecture.title: Merkle trees
lecture.say: A merkle tree squeezes thousands of transactions into one hash that sits in the header. This part builds a small tree, follows a short proof that one transaction is inside, and meets a weakness that comes from repeating the last hash. The three columns preview the part: the tree of hashes with example 9, short proofs with examples 10 and 12, and the weakness with example 11. Ralph Merkle's patent of 1982, told on slide 25, is the source of the idea. Remember that the header commits to the root, not to the list of transactions itself.
lecture.takeaway: A merkle tree ends in one hash, the root, that stands for every transaction

lecture.title: Merkle trees: key concepts (1 of 2)
lecture.say: These cards define the tree. A merkle tree is a tree of hashes in which each parent hashes its two children and the top is a single root; in a binary tree every node has two children, so a tree over many leaves is only a few levels deep; a balanced tree pads an odd level by repeating its last hash so that every level pairs up; and a light client keeps only headers and asks for a short proof that a transaction is in a block. Example 9 builds the levels and example 12 shows the light client. The weakness of the padding is the subject of example 11 on slide 26.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: Pair, hash, repeat
lecture.say: Four transaction ids of a private block form the bottom level of the tree. Hashing them in pairs gives two hashes, and hashing those gives the root, which equals the value in the block header; the levels hold 4, 2 and 1 hashes. With three ids the last one is paired with itself, which gives levels of 3, 2 and 1 and still a single root. The padding detail causes the weakness shown in example 11. This is example 9. Compare the proof size on slide 24 and the light client on slide 27.
lecture.takeaway: An odd level is completed by pairing the last hash with itself

lecture.title: Merkle trees: key concepts (2 of 2)
lecture.say: Three cards describe how a membership proof works. The authentication path is the list of sibling hashes from a leaf up to the root, and with them anyone can recompute the root; the merkle path is another name for the same list, one sibling hash for each level, so there are not two ideas; and lightweight clients are wallets that download headers only and verify transactions with merkle proofs. Example 10 builds a path and example 12 parses a proof sent to a light client. Retell in your own words why a verifier needs the siblings and not the whole list.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: A proof of four hashes
lecture.say: To prove that one of sixteen transactions is in a block, the prover hands over the sibling hash at each level: four hashes of 32 bytes, 128 bytes in all. Following them upward rebuilds the root in the header. The proof grows with the logarithm of the number of transactions, so 1,024 transactions need 320 bytes, 4,096 need 384 and 16,000 need 448, which is 14 hashes. Each doubling of the block adds a single hash. This is example 10, and the slow growth is what makes the light clients of slide 27 possible.
lecture.takeaway: The proof grows slowly: 16,000 transactions need 14 hashes

lecture.title: Ralph Merkle's hash tree
lecture.say: On 5 January 1982 the United States published patent 4,309,569, Method of providing digital signatures, by Ralph Merkle, with the Board of Trustees of Stanford University as assignee; his hash tree dates from 1979. The idea is small and strong: one short root vouches for a long list. Decades later the same idea sits in every Bitcoin block, where a header, which has room for one hash, covers every transaction. In block 277,315 the 40 transaction ids were hashed in pairs, six levels up, until a single root sat in the header. The source line names the patent number and the date, so the story can be checked.
lecture.takeaway: One small hash that vouches for a whole list

lecture.title: Two lists, one root
lecture.say: Two different lists can have the same merkle root. When a level has an odd number of hashes, the last one is paired with itself, so a list that already repeats its last ids, as the six transactions here become eight, builds the same pairs and the same root. A block that carries such a copy would look valid by its header. Core received a mutated block of four transactions in place of the original three, rejected it with the verdict bad-txns-duplicate, and the original stayed the tip. The defence works on the content of the block and not on its header. This is example 11, the first weakness of the tree. Compare the padding rule on slide 22 and the Optech topic on slide 42.
lecture.takeaway: Core refuses a block whose transaction list repeats a hash

lecture.title: A light client needs 248 bytes
lecture.say: A light client asks a full node for a proof instead of the whole block. The merkleblock message holds the header, a count of transactions, five hashes and some flag bits, 248 bytes in all for a block of sixteen transactions, and it shows that one transaction is in the block. Bitcoin Core confirmed that the proof names exactly the transaction that was asked about. For blocks with thousands of transactions the saving is much larger, because a proof grows by only one hash for each doubling. This is example 12; it uses the path idea of slide 24.
lecture.takeaway: A phone can check one payment without the other fifteen transactions

lecture.title: Test blockchains
lecture.say: Bitcoin has more than one chain. Testnet, signet and regtest follow the same rules as the main chain but use different constants, so developers can experiment without real money. This part compares the five chains and reads their constants, tells why testnet3 was replaced, and opens signet's challenge script. The three columns preview the part: the five chains in example 13, testnet and its flooding problem in example 14, and signet and regtest in examples 16 and 17. Remember that the rules are shared and only the constants and the value of the coins differ.
lecture.takeaway: A test chain has its own rules, its own ports and no real money

lecture.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (1 of 5)
lecture.say: These cards introduce the test chains. Bitcoin's test blockchains are separate chains with Bitcoin's rules and worthless coins; testnet is the public one, and its coins have no value; using testnet means pointing a wallet or node at it and taking free coins from a faucet; and its minimum-difficulty rule let miners flood it with blocks, which is why testnet4 replaced it. Example 13 reads the constants, example 14 the rule, and the story on slide 33 tells the flood. Retell what is the same and what differs between a test chain and mainnet.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: One code base, five chains
lecture.say: The constants of every chain live in one source file, chainparams.cpp. Each chain listens on its own default port: 8333 for mainnet, 18333 for the old testnet, 48333 for testnet4, 38333 for signet and 18444 for regtest, so nodes of different chains do not mix. The size of the data that a new node is assumed to download ranges from 856 gigabytes for main through 245 for test, 31 for testnet4 and 24 for signet down to 0 for regtest. This is example 13. The saved source files are listed in the references of the course page.
lecture.takeaway: Each chain has its own port, so nodes of different chains never mix

lecture.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (2 of 5)
lecture.say: These cards describe the controlled test chains. Signet needs a signature from a trusted signer on every block, so the chain stays calm; one default signet is maintained and anyone can start another with their own challenge script; regtest is a private chain on your own computer where blocks are mined on demand; and development follows the order build on regtest, try on signet or testnet, release on mainnet. Example 16 opens the challenge script and example 17 shows the halving of regtest. Retell which test chain suits trying a wallet feature on a laptop, and why.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: Testnet allows easy blocks
lecture.say: Testnet allows a block at the minimum difficulty after twenty idle minutes. The result shows that testnet, testnet4 and regtest allow this and that mainnet and signet do not. The rule keeps a quiet test chain moving, but it also let miners flood testnet3 with blocks. Bitcoin Core's help text now says that support for testnet3 is deprecated, and testnet4 starts again from a new genesis block whose hash starts with 00000000da. This is example 14; the story on slide 33 explains why the rule became a problem.
lecture.takeaway: Two of the test chains may drop to the easiest difficulty after twenty minutes

lecture.title: When testnet was flooded with blocks
lecture.say: On 4 May 2024 Jameson Lopp published Griefing Bitcoin's Testnet and explained how the testnet3 rule, easy blocks after twenty idle minutes, let miners create hundreds of blocks in a single day. A rule meant to keep a small chain moving had become an invitation to vandals, because test coins cost nothing. Fabian Jahr's BIP 94 and testnet4 write rules against abuse into the chain itself; BIP 94 notes that three years of blocks were mined in a few weeks. On 15 October 2026 testnet3 stood at height 5,189,394 and testnet4 at 156,618. The source line leads to BIP 94. Compare signet on slide 38, another answer.
lecture.takeaway: A test network without incentives gets flooded

lecture.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (3 of 5)
lecture.say: This recap defines three terms. Test blockchains are chains that follow Bitcoin's rules with different constants; testnet is the public test chain, and the current one is testnet4; signet is a test chain in which each block must carry a valid signature. The rules are the same as on mainnet, while the constants and the value of the coins differ. Examples 13 to 15 compare the constants, and example 16 opens the challenge that decides who may sign. Retell, without looking, what is the same and what differs between a test chain and mainnet.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: Addresses show the chain
lecture.say: Every chain writes its addresses with a prefix of its own. Mainnet uses bc for SegWit addresses and version byte 0 for legacy ones; testnet, testnet4 and signet use tb and 111; regtest uses bcrt and 111. Bitcoin Core made a real regtest address that starts with bcrt1q, so the prefix in the table is the one that the software produces. A wallet can reject an address of the wrong chain at once, which protects against sending real money to a test address. This is example 15; the earlier chapter on keys and addresses explains the formats.
lecture.takeaway: A testnet address can never be mistaken for a real one

lecture.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (4 of 5)
lecture.say: These cards connect the signet vocabulary. The default signet is the public signet that most developers share; custom signets are created by choosing your own challenge script; and the challenge script is the script that a signet block's signature must satisfy. Changing the script gives another network, because the four magic bytes, the fixed first bytes of every message that the nodes of a network send each other, come from its hash. Example 16 opens the default challenge of 71 bytes. Retell how the challenge script, the chain and its magic bytes depend on each other.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: Signet: a challenge script
lecture.say: The default signet's challenge is a short script of 71 bytes that asks for a signature from one of two keys, a one-of-two multisig. The four message-start bytes, the fixed first bytes of every message between the nodes of a network, 0a03cf40, are the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of that script written with its length byte in front, so a different challenge gives a different network: a challenge of 51, which is OP_TRUE and lets anyone sign, gives 54d26fbd. This is example 16. BIP 325 defines the rules, and the chapters on scripts and signatures explain multisig and the checks behind a signature.
lecture.takeaway: The four magic bytes come from the hash of the length-prefixed challenge

lecture.title: A test network where signatures replace mining
lecture.say: On 20 March 2019 BIP 325, by Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns, was assigned; it defines signet, a test network in which a signature replaces mining. Every signet has a challenge, a locking script, and a block is valid only if it carries a solution to it, so only the holders of the matching keys can make blocks. The default challenge is a one-of-two multisig, unlocked by a signature from either of two keys. The four magic bytes that start every network message, 0a03cf40, are the first four bytes of the double SHA-256 of that script with its length byte in front. Nobody can flood it, so it stays calm, at the price of open participation. Core 0.21.0 added signet; on 15 October 2026 its tip was at height 326,440, 2.27 times the 143,619 blocks of the book's listing.
lecture.takeaway: Replace mining by a signature and the test network stays calm

lecture.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (5 of 5)
lecture.say: The last concept cards anchor three terms. Regtest is the regression-test mode: a private chain with trivial difficulty; BIP 325 is the proposal that defines signet; and mainnet is the real Bitcoin chain, where coins have value. Place each activity on the right chain: trying a script belongs on regtest, trying a shared setup on signet, and paying real money on mainnet. Example 17 shows the halving of regtest and example 15 shows that mainnet addresses start with bc. Retell how the three terms relate.
lecture.takeaway: Each card gives one idea as one plain sentence

lecture.title: Halving every 150 blocks
lecture.say: On regtest the reward halves every 150 blocks instead of every 210,000, so the whole schedule can be tested in seconds. The code feeds 150 to the library's rule and obtains 50, 50, 25, 25, 12.5 and 6.25 coins at the heights 1, 149, 150, 299, 300 and 450. The same rule gives the same numbers as the record of the 500 blocks that Bitcoin Core mined. A shorter schedule is a changed constant, not a different rule. This is example 17; the real schedule is explained in the mining chapter of Mastering Bitcoin.
lecture.takeaway: Mine 500 blocks in seconds and see the reward halve three times

lecture.title: The chapter in five lines
lecture.say: These five lines are the chapter in miniature. One: a block is an 80-byte header of six fields plus its transactions, named by the double hash of the header. Two: each header names its parent, so changing an old block breaks every later link, and a fork ends when one branch is longer. Three: a merkle tree puts all transactions under one root, and a short path proves one of them. Four: repeating the last hash can give two lists one root, and Core refuses the copy. Five: testnet, signet and regtest share the rules and differ in constants. The header slides, the fork slides, the merkle path, the weakness slide and the test chain slides prove them in that order; run each example in the Run slide code menu. Compare with the seven questions of slide 3.
lecture.takeaway: If a line feels unproven, the code slide of its part holds the proof

lecture.title: Where to go from here
lecture.say: Everything here is free to read or watch, and every link was opened on the date in the subtitle. The Optech topics explain merkle tree vulnerabilities and signet, mempool.space lets you look up any block on the real chain, BIP 94 and BIP 325 are the specifications behind testnet4 and signet, and the white paper is Nakamoto's nine pages of October 2008. The visual demo by Anders Brownworth shows hashing, blocks and chains step by step. The community entries, the weekly Optech newsletter, Delving Bitcoin and the bitcoin-dev mailing list, are where proposals are debated and questions get answered after the course.
